# RevOps vs Sales Ops: What Changed and Why It Matters

Source: https://lowob.com/research/revops-vs-sales-ops/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Sales operations (sales ops) is the function that gives a sales team its processes, tools, data and plans: territories, quotas, compensation, CRM administration and the forecast. Revenue operations (RevOps) runs the same kind of work across the whole revenue line, so marketing, sales and customer success share one set of definitions, one data model and one set of systems. The change is one of scope and ownership. It matters more now because AI tools read across all three functions and inherit every disagreement between them.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## Key points

- Gartner describes sales operations as providing "the resources, processes, analytics and decision support needed to succeed".
- Gartner describes revenue operations as "the modern operating model for driving efficient, predictable revenue", built on an end-to-end process across go-to-market functions.
- In 2021 Gartner predicted that by 2025, 75% of the highest growth companies would deploy a RevOps model. It was a prediction, not a measured result.
- Forrester, writing about Asia Pacific firms, notes that RevOps work may sit in a dedicated team or in existing sales and marketing operations teams.
- In **lowob**'s brain loop, RevOps owns the definitions in the store, the wiring between systems and the outcome write-back that drives learning.

## What the two terms mean

**Sales operations** grew up to make a sales team efficient. Gartner's description covers designing and managing the team that supports the revenue process, improving sales analytics and data quality, raising data literacy among sellers and managers, and designing compensation plans and quotas. In practice a sales ops lead owns the CRM configuration, territory design, pipeline reporting and the forecast cadence. The customer is the sales leader.

**Revenue operations** takes the same disciplines and applies them to every function that touches revenue. Gartner frames it as one operating model organised into strategy, process, workflow, data, analysis and technology across go-to-market teams. Forrester's definition is "a highly configured, iterative commercial execution strategy designed to maximize customer value and company performance." Our explainer on [revenue operations](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-revenue-operations/) covers the function in more depth. Here the question is what differs from sales ops.

| Dimension | Sales ops | RevOps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | The sales team | Marketing, sales and customer success, sometimes partners |
| Main customer | Head of sales | Chief revenue officer or chief executive |
| Owns definitions of | Opportunity stages, forecast categories | The whole customer lifecycle, from lead to renewal |
| Systems owned | CRM and sales tools | The go-to-market stack and the data flowing between tools |
| Typical metrics | Pipeline coverage, win rate, quota attainment | The same, plus conversion across functions, retention and net revenue retention |
| Planning | Territories, quotas, compensation | Capacity and targets across all revenue teams |
| Typical failure | Optimises sales while marketing and success use other numbers | Becomes a reporting team without authority to change process |

## What changed, and why

The shift was a response to handoffs. Gartner's 2021 announcement argued that separate departments passing customers between each other, each with its own tools and methods, slow revenue growth. Its answer was to align sales, marketing and customer success technology, data and KPIs so the revenue process can be managed as one system.

Three changes follow from that.

**One set of definitions.** A marketing-qualified lead, a sales-accepted opportunity and a renewal at risk are defined once, in writing, and every system uses them. Without that, marketing reports leads that sales does not recognise, and customer success forecasts renewals on criteria nobody else sees. Clear [pipeline stage definitions](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/) are the usual starting point.

**One data model.** Accounts, contacts and deals link across the marketing tool, the CRM and the customer success platform. Recurring revenue made this more pressing: in a subscription business, much of the revenue arrives after the sale, in renewals and expansion that sales ops never owned.

**One owner for the stack.** Tools are bought and configured against the whole process, not team by team.

Forrester's point about structure, made about Asia Pacific organisations, is worth noting for smaller firms. RevOps does not always mean a new department. In some firms a separate team takes on the work; in others, existing sales and marketing operations teams expand their remit.

## Why it matters more with AI

AI assistants and agents make the difference between the two models visible. An assistant preparing a renewal brief reads marketing engagement, the sales history and support tickets. If those three systems define "active customer" differently, the brief is confidently wrong. An agent that updates CRM fields after calls needs to know which definitions and fields it may touch, and who owns them.

Under a pure sales ops model, nobody owns the seams between functions. Under RevOps, someone does. That is why we treat RevOps as the natural owner of the work described in [AI Agents in Commercial Operations](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-commercial-operations/): hygiene, routing, forecast preparation and the records agents depend on.

## Which model fits

A renamed team with the same remit is still sales ops. The test is scope and authority, not title.

| Signal in your firm | Model that fits |
| --- | --- |
| Sales is the only go-to-market motion and marketing is small | Sales ops, with clear definitions shared with marketing |
| Leadership disputes lead or pipeline numbers every month | RevOps, starting with shared definitions |
| A large share of revenue comes from renewals and expansion | RevOps, so customer success data is part of the model |
| Each team buys and configures its own tools | RevOps, with one owner for the stack |
| AI assistants or agents read across more than one function | RevOps, or at least one named owner of cross-system definitions |
| Under about 50 people, one ops generalist | Either label; give that person the remit across all functions |

A short checklist for a firm moving from sales ops to RevOps:

- **Write the lifecycle definitions first.** Lead to renewal, on one page, signed off by each function head.
- **Give the role authority over process.** A RevOps team that can only report will not fix handoffs.
- **Map every system to the facts it owns.** One home per fact, as in [CRM vs CDP vs Data Warehouse](https://lowob.com/research/crm-vs-cdp-vs-data-warehouse/).
- **Decide who records commercial decisions.** Discounts, exceptions and priority calls need an owner and a reason.

## The **lowob** view

The enterprise brain is a loop: store, wiring, record, reasoning, learning. Sales ops maintains one part of the store, the CRM, for one team. RevOps is the function best placed to own the definitions across the whole store and the wiring that connects marketing, sales and customer success systems.

It is also the natural keeper of the record and the learning stage. A record of [commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/), each with a reason, owner, status and expected outcome, needs a function that spans the revenue line. So does writing outcomes back: whether the discount won the deal, whether the at-risk renewal held. Those results are what make the next forecast and the next agent draft better.

Rent the tools. Have RevOps own the definitions, the decision record and the write-back, because those are what any AI the firm adopts will depend on.

## lowob takeaways

- **The difference is scope.** Sales ops serves sales; RevOps serves the whole revenue line.
- **Handoffs drove the change.** Separate tools and numbers between functions slow revenue.
- **AI raises the stakes.** Assistants and agents read across functions and inherit their inconsistencies.
- **Authority beats the title.** RevOps needs the remit to change process, not only to report on it.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between RevOps and sales ops?

Sales ops supports the sales team with processes, tools, data and plans. RevOps does that work across marketing, sales and customer success, with shared definitions, data and systems.

### Does RevOps replace sales operations?

Often it absorbs it. Sales operations work such as territories, quotas and the forecast continues inside a wider RevOps remit, sometimes run by the same people.

### When should a company move from sales ops to RevOps?

When functions dispute each other's numbers, when renewals and expansion are a large share of revenue, or when tools and AI systems need to read across teams.
